brief: Propose how the package manager should resolve conflicting version constraints between two dependencies. Reviewers will compare against the current behaviour, which fails the install.
strong:
# Conflict resolution by backtracking

## Proposal

When two dependencies require incompatible versions of a package, the resolver backtracks to the most recent choice that can be changed and tries the next candidate version, failing only when every combination has been tried.

## Rationale

Failing the install, the current behaviour, forces users to pin versions by hand even when a compatible set exists. Backtracking finds that set when it exists.

## Alternatives

Installing both versions side by side avoids search but breaks languages with a single global module namespace, which ours has. A SAT solver gives the same answers with better worst-case behaviour but adds a large dependency; we keep it as a fallback if backtracking proves slow on real lockfiles.

## Drawbacks

Worst-case resolution time is exponential; we cap search at 10,000 steps and then report the conflict as today.
weak:
# Conflict resolution by backtracking

## Proposal

When two dependencies require incompatible versions of a package, the resolver backtracks to the most recent choice that can be changed and tries the next candidate version, failing only when every combination has been tried.

## Rationale

Backtracking is the standard approach and is the best way to resolve conflicts.

## Implementation

Store choices on a stack of (package, candidates_iterator) tuples. On conflict, pop until an iterator yields a new candidate, push it, and re-run constraint propagation from that frame. Use a dict for the propagated constraints and copy it on push.

## Drawbacks

Worst-case resolution time is exponential; we cap search at 10,000 steps and then report the conflict as today.
